questions.title: M2 receptor activation on the heart decreases cAMP
questions.question: Activation of postsynaptic M2 receptors on the heart is associated with

explanations.A: Correct. M2 muscarinic receptors on the heart are Gi-protein coupled. Their activation inhibits adenylate cyclase, decreasing intracellular cAMP. This produces the receptor's negative chronotropic (heart-rate-slowing) effect.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Opening of Na+/K+ cation channels describes nicotinic (ligand-gated) receptor signalling, not the G-protein-coupled M2 muscarinic receptor.
explanations.C: Incorrect. M2 receptor activation inhibits, rather than activates, adenylyl cyclase -- activation of adenylyl cyclase is instead the pattern of a Gs-coupled receptor such as cardiac beta-1.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Increased IP3 and DAG is the Gq-coupled M3 receptor's signalling pattern, not the Gi-coupled M2 receptor found in the heart.
explanations.E: Incorrect. M2 receptor signalling does not work through protein kinase C at all -- that pathway belongs to Gq-coupled receptors like M3, not the Gi-coupled M2.

questions.title: Neurotransmitter at the sympathetic ganglion is ACh
questions.question: Which of the following is correct regarding the autonomic nervous system (ANS)?

options.A: Sympathetic neurons release ACh in the effector organs.
options.B: The neurotransmitter at the sympathetic ganglion is acetylcholine (ACh).
options.C: Parasympathetic neurons release NE in the effector organs.
options.D: The neurotransmitter at the parasympathetic ganglion is norepinephrine (NE).

explanations.A: Incorrect. Sympathetic postganglionic neurons release noradrenaline (NE), not ACh, at most effector organs -- ACh is used only at the sweat-gland and skeletal-muscle-vasodilator exceptions.
explanations.B: Correct. Every preganglionic autonomic fibre, sympathetic and parasympathetic alike, is cholinergic. So the neurotransmitter at the sympathetic ganglion (the preganglionic-to-postganglionic synapse) is acetylcholine. It acts there on nicotinic receptors.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Parasympathetic postganglionic neurons release ACh, not NE, at the effector organs -- every postganglionic parasympathetic fibre is cholinergic.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The neurotransmitter at the parasympathetic ganglion is acetylcholine, not norepinephrine -- all preganglionic autonomic fibres, including parasympathetic ones, are cholinergic.

questions.learning_objective: State that the neurotransmitter at the sympathetic ganglion is acetylcholine.
questions.module_subject: AUN-MPT-104 > Pharmacology > Introduction to Autonomic Nervous System

field_notes.keySource: printed "The correct answer is: The neurotransmitter at the sympathetic ganglion is acetylcholine (ACh)."

questions.title: M2 cholinoreceptor location: the heart
questions.question: Indicate the location of M2 cholinoreceptor type:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Glandular tissue is characteristically M3, not M2, muscarinic receptor territory -- M3 receptors there signal through IP3/DAG to drive secretion.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Smooth muscle (for example bronchiolar or GI smooth muscle) is characteristically M3 receptor territory, not M2 -- M2 receptors are the cardiac subtype.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Vascular endothelium expresses muscarinic receptors that trigger nitric-oxide-mediated vasodilation, a role distinct from the cardiac M2 subtype.
explanations.D: Correct. M2 muscarinic receptors are the cardiac subtype. They are Gi-protein coupled and decrease cAMP. This slows the heart rate, a negative chronotropic effect.

questions.title: ACh not a specific transmitter at sympathetic postganglionic endings
questions.question: Acetylcholine is not a specific neurotransmitter at:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Acetylcholine IS the specific transmitter at parasympathetic postganglionic nerve endings -- every postganglionic parasympathetic fibre is cholinergic, so this is not the exception being asked for.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Acetylcholine IS the specific transmitter at parasympathetic ganglia -- all preganglionic autonomic fibres, including parasympathetic ones, are cholinergic.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Acetylcholine IS the specific transmitter at sympathetic ganglia too -- ganglionic transmission is cholinergic for both divisions, so this is not the exception.
explanations.D: Correct. Sympathetic postganglionic nerve endings are the one site where acetylcholine is not the specific transmitter. Most release noradrenaline instead. Only the sweat-gland and skeletal-muscle-vasodilator fibres remain cholinergic exceptions.

questions.learning_objective: Identify sympathetic postganglionic nerve endings as the site where acetylcholine is not the specific transmitter.

questions.title: Transmitters at each stage of autonomic outflow
questions.question: Preganglionic sympathetic and parasympathetic fibers release -----, postganglionic parasympathetic fibers release ----- (for muscarinic cholinergic receptors), and postganglionic sympathetic fibers release -------- (for adrenergic receptors).

explanations.A: Incorrect. Preganglionic fibres of both divisions release ACh (correct for the first blank), but postganglionic parasympathetic fibres also release ACh, not NE -- this option reverses the second blank.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Preganglionic fibres of both divisions release ACh, not NE -- this option gets the first blank backwards.
explanations.C: Correct. All preganglionic autonomic fibres are cholinergic and release ACh. Postganglionic parasympathetic fibres are also cholinergic and release ACh, acting on muscarinic receptors. Postganglionic sympathetic fibres, however, switch transmitter and release noradrenaline (NE), acting on adrenergic receptors.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Preganglionic fibres release ACh, not NE, and postganglionic parasympathetic fibres release ACh, not NE -- this option has both of the first two blanks backwards.

questions.title: Pyogenic inflammation leads to suppuration
questions.question: Pyogenic inflammation often leads to:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Catarrhal inflammation is defined by excess mucosal secretion, not by pus formation, so it is not the typical outcome of a pyogenic (pus-forming organism) infection.
explanations.B: Correct. Pyogenic organisms are, by definition, pus-producing. Their infection typically leads to suppurative inflammation. That is acute inflammation with a substantial purulent, neutrophil-rich exudate.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Tumour formation is an unrelated, non-inflammatory process, not a typical consequence of pyogenic infection.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Gangrene is tissue death from ischaemia or specific necrotising infection, a different process from the purulent-exudate pattern that defines suppurative inflammation.

questions.learning_objective: State that pyogenic inflammation typically leads to suppurative inflammation.

field_notes.keySource: printed "The correct answer is: Suppurative inflammation"

questions.title: Why cellulitis spreads diffusely
questions.question: Which of the following is the cause of the diffuse nature of cellulitis?

options.C: Production of fibrinolysin and hyaluronidase by the organism
options.E: Excess fibrin in the inflammatory exudate

explanations.A: Incorrect. Poor patient resistance is a general risk factor for infection severity, not the specific mechanism that makes cellulitis spread diffusely rather than stay localized.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Inoculum size affects whether infection takes hold, but it is not what determines the diffuse, unwalled-off spreading pattern specifically.
explanations.C: Correct. Streptococcus pyogenes, the organism typically causing cellulitis, secretes fibrinolysin, which breaks down the fibrin that would otherwise wall off the infection. It also secretes hyaluronidase, a spreading factor that breaks down connective-tissue ground substance. Together these let the infection spread diffusely instead of being localized.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Loose tissue is where cellulitis characteristically occurs, but the tissue location is a site, not the causal mechanism of diffuse spread -- the organism's own enzymes are the cause.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Cellulitis is characterized by a lack of walling-off fibrin (because fibrinolysin breaks it down), not by excess fibrin -- excess fibrin would instead favour localization, as in an abscess.

questions.learning_objective: State that streptococcal fibrinolysin and hyaluronidase are what cause cellulitis's diffuse spread.

field_notes.keySource: printed "The correct answer is: Production of fibrinolysin and hyaluronidase by the organism"

questions.title: Localized suppurative inflammation with multiple sinuses
questions.question: A localized suppurative with multiple sinuses is called:

explanations.A: Incorrect. A simple abscess is a single, discrete, walled-off collection of pus, not one that drains through multiple sinuses.
explanations.B: Correct. A carbuncle is a localized suppurative infection, walled off like an abscess by staphylococcal coagulase. Unlike a simple abscess, though, it involves multiple adjacent hair follicles. It drains through several sinus tracts rather than a single cavity.
explanations.C: Incorrect. A furuncle (boil) is a localized suppurative infection of a single hair follicle, without the multiple interconnected sinuses that define a carbuncle.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Cellulitis is the diffuse, not localized, pattern of suppurative inflammation, spread by streptococcal fibrinolysin and hyaluronidase rather than walled off into sinuses.

questions.learning_objective: Identify a carbuncle as a localized suppurative infection draining through multiple sinuses.

questions.title: Cellulitis is caused by streptococci
questions.question: Cellulitis is caused by:

explanations.A: Correct. Cellulitis is the diffuse pattern of suppurative inflammation. It is commonly caused by Streptococcus pyogenes (haemolyticus). That organism's fibrinolysin and hyaluronidase let the infection spread rather than being walled off.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Klebsiella is not the organism typically named for cellulitis in this teaching pattern -- it is streptococci whose enzymes explain the diffuse spread.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Clostridia are associated with gas gangrene and other necrotizing/toxin-mediated processes, not with the diffuse suppurative pattern of cellulitis.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Staphylococcus aureus, via coagulase, is the organism associated with localized suppuration (abscess, furuncle, carbuncle), not diffuse cellulitis.

questions.learning_objective: State that streptococci are the organism typically causing cellulitis.

questions.title: Carbuncle is a localized suppuration
questions.question: Carbuncle is a:

explanations.A: Incorrect. A carbuncle is not defined by haemorrhage -- it is a purulent, pus-forming lesion, not a bleeding one.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Catarrhal inflammation is excess mucosal secretion, an entirely different pattern from a carbuncle's purulent, localized suppuration.
explanations.C: Incorrect. A carbuncle is localized, walled off by staphylococcal coagulase, not diffuse -- diffuse suppuration (cellulitis) is the streptococcal, fibrinolysin-driven pattern instead.
explanations.D: Correct. A carbuncle is a localized suppurative infection. Like an abscess or furuncle, it is walled off by staphylococcal coagulase. Unlike either, it involves multiple adjacent follicles draining through several sinuses.

questions.learning_objective: Classify a carbuncle as a localized, not diffuse, suppuration.

questions.title: Cellulitis occurs in loose tissues
questions.question: Cellulitis is characterized by:

options.C: Inflammatory cells include plasma cells and lymphocytes

explanations.A: Correct. Cellulitis is the diffuse pattern of suppurative inflammation. It characteristically occurs in loose connective tissue -- subcutaneous tissue, the orbit, the scrotum. Fibrinolysin-driven spread meets little resistance there.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Staphylococcus aureus is associated with the localized pattern (abscess, furuncle, carbuncle), not with diffuse cellulitis, which is typically streptococcal.
explanations.C: Incorrect. An acute suppurative exudate, including in cellulitis, is neutrophil-rich, not rich in plasma cells and lymphocytes -- those instead characterise chronic inflammation.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Inflammation centred around hair follicles describes a furuncle or carbuncle (localized suppuration), not diffuse cellulitis of loose tissue.

questions.learning_objective: State that cellulitis characteristically occurs in loose tissues.

field_notes.keySource: printed "The correct answer is: Occurs in loose tissues"

questions.title: Mushroom pilocarpine ingestion causes diarrhea
questions.question: Which one of the following effects is caused by the ingestion of mushrooms that contain pilocarpine?

explanations.A: Incorrect. As a muscarinic agonist, pilocarpine causes bronchoconstriction, not bronchodilation.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Muscarinic stimulation from pilocarpine tends to lower, not raise, blood pressure via vasodilation, not cause hypertension.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Pilocarpine's muscarinic effects include increased sweating, but it does not characteristically cause hyperthermia.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Muscarinic (M2) stimulation of the heart slows, rather than speeds, the heart rate, so pilocarpine ingestion would tend toward bradycardia, not tachycardia.
explanations.E: Correct. Pilocarpine is a direct muscarinic agonist. Muscarinic stimulation of GI smooth muscle increases motility and secretion. This produces diarrhoea, among the classic muscarinic-excess effects of ingesting pilocarpine-containing mushrooms.

questions.learning_objective: State that pilocarpine ingestion causes diarrhoea via muscarinic GI stimulation.

questions.title: Parasympathomimetics cause bradycardia
questions.question: Parasympathomimetic drugs cause:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Parasympathomimetics cause bronchoconstriction (via M3 receptors on airway smooth muscle), not bronchodilation.
explanations.B: Correct. Parasympathomimetics stimulate M2 muscarinic receptors on the heart. These receptors are Gi-coupled and decrease cAMP. That produces a negative chronotropic effect: bradycardia.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Parasympathomimetics increase, rather than decrease, GI motility, producing diarrhoea rather than constipation.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Parasympathomimetics cause miosis (pupillary constriction), not mydriasis, which is instead an antimuscarinic effect.

questions.title: Pilocarpine is used to decrease IOP
questions.question: Pilocarpine is most commonly used for?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Lowering blood pressure is not pilocarpine's characteristic clinical use -- its two established indications are as a sialagogue for xerostomia and a miotic for glaucoma.
explanations.B: Correct. Pilocarpine, a direct muscarinic agonist, is used topically as a miotic for glaucoma. It contracts the ciliary muscle and iris sphincter. This opens the trabecular drainage angle, lowering intraocular pressure.
explanations.C: Incorrect. While muscarinic stimulation can slow the heart via M2 receptors, decreasing heart rate is not pilocarpine's characteristic clinical indication -- its established uses are ocular (glaucoma) and glandular (xerostomia).
explanations.D: Incorrect. Urinary retention is treated with a different direct-acting muscarinic agonist, bethanechol, selective for GI/bladder smooth muscle -- not pilocarpine's characteristic indication.

questions.learning_objective: State that pilocarpine's most common clinical use is decreasing intraocular pressure in glaucoma.

questions.title: Rivastigmine is a reversible AChE inhibitor
questions.question: What type of drug is rivastigmine?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Rivastigmine is an anticholinesterase, not a muscarinic antagonist -- it raises acetylcholine levels rather than blocking muscarinic receptors.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Rivastigmine forms a temporary enzyme complex and its inhibition wanes over time -- it is reversible, unlike an organophosphate-type agent such as echothiophate.
explanations.C: Correct. Rivastigmine is a reversible acetylcholinesterase inhibitor used specifically for Alzheimer's disease. It raises acetylcholine at central cholinergic synapses. This partly offsets the cholinergic-neuron loss underlying the disease's cognitive decline.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Rivastigmine acts on the cholinergic, not adrenergic, system -- it is an anticholinesterase, not an adrenergic agonist.

questions.learning_objective: Classify rivastigmine as a reversible acetylcholinesterase inhibitor.

questions.title: Alzheimer's disease strategy: inhibit acetylcholinesterase
questions.question: In Alzheimers disease, there is a deficiency of cholinergic neuronal function in the brain. Theoretically, which of the following strategies will be useful in treating the symptoms of Alzheimers disease?

options.A: Inhibiting the acetylcholinesterase enzyme in the brain.
options.B: Activating the acetylcholinesterase enzyme in the brain.
options.C: Inhibiting the release of acetylcholine in the brain.
options.D: Inhibiting cholinergic receptors in the brain.

explanations.A: Correct. Inhibiting acetylcholinesterase, as rivastigmine and other anticholinesterases used for Alzheimer's disease do, raises acetylcholine at central cholinergic synapses. This partly offsets the cholinergic-neuron loss and deficiency underlying the disease. It is the rational pharmacological strategy for treating its cognitive symptoms.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Activating acetylcholinesterase would further deplete, not restore, acetylcholine levels -- the opposite of what a cholinergic-deficiency disease needs.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Inhibiting acetylcholine release would worsen, not treat, a cholinergic deficiency state.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Inhibiting cholinergic receptors would block the effect of whatever acetylcholine remains, worsening rather than treating the deficiency.

questions.learning_objective: State that inhibiting acetylcholinesterase is the theoretical strategy for treating Alzheimer's disease symptoms.

field_notes.keySource: printed "The correct answer is: Inhibiting the acetylcholinesterase enzyme in the brain."

questions.title: Reversible cholinesterase inhibitor for Alzheimer's: rivastigmine
questions.question: Which of the following reversible cholinesterase inhibitors is used for Alzheimer disease?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Edrophonium's reversible inhibition is far too brief for maintenance Alzheimer's therapy -- its niche is diagnostic (the Tensilon test for myasthenic vs cholinergic crisis), not Alzheimer's treatment.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Pyridostigmine's reversible inhibition is used for myasthenia gravis and neuromuscular blocker reversal, not for Alzheimer's disease.
explanations.C: Correct. Rivastigmine is the reversible acetylcholinesterase inhibitor used specifically for Alzheimer's disease. It is distinct in indication from the other reversible inhibitors listed here. Each of pyridostigmine, edrophonium and neostigmine instead has its own separate clinical niche (myasthenia gravis, diagnosis, or NMJ block reversal).
explanations.D: Incorrect. Neostigmine's reversible inhibition is used for myasthenia gravis, neuromuscular blocker reversal, and postoperative ileus/urinary retention -- not for Alzheimer's disease.

questions.learning_objective: Identify rivastigmine as the reversible cholinesterase inhibitor used for Alzheimer's disease.

questions.title: Best combination for organophosphate poisoning treatment
questions.question: In case of organophosphate insecticide poisoning, which of the following drug combination is the most effective treatment?

explanations.A: Correct. The standard management protocol pairs pralidoxime's enzyme-reactivating action, restoring acetylcholinesterase before the phosphorylated enzyme 'ages', with atropine's competitive antimuscarinic blockade of the poisoning's excess acetylcholine. Both are given concurrently. A benzodiazepine for seizure control is added to this same protocol.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Physostigmine is itself a reversible acetylcholinesterase inhibitor -- adding it would worsen, not treat, the acetylcholinesterase-inhibitor poisoning, rather than reversing it as atropine does.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Physostigmine would worsen the poisoning as in option B, and propranolol (a beta-blocker) plays no established role in organophosphate poisoning management.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Propranolol is not part of the standard protocol, and this combination omits pralidoxime, the agent that reactivates the poisoned acetylcholinesterase enzyme itself.

questions.learning_objective: State that atropine plus pralidoxime is the most effective combination for organophosphate poisoning.

field_notes.keySource: printed "The correct answer is: Atropine and pralidoxime"
